name: Chang Chi
bio: Chang Chi is dated by Giles to the 8th and 9th centuries AD. His poem here is a wife’s answer to an admirer, a favourite theme of the T’ang quatrain.
The poems here are Herbert A. Giles’s versions in Chinese Poetry in English Verse (1898), given with the poet’s name as spelled in that book.

poems.title: The Chaste Wife's Reply
poems.author: Chang Chi
poems.text:
Knowing, fair sir, my matrimonial thrall,
Two pearls thou sentest me, costly withal.
And I, seeing that Love thy heart possessed,
I wrapped them coldly in my silken vest.

For mine is a household of high degree.
My husband captain in the King's army;
And one with wit like thine should say,
"The troth of wives is for ever and ay."

With thy two pearls I send thee back two tears:
Tears — that we did not meet in earlier years!

poems.title: Thinking of a Friend Lost in the Tibetan War
poems.author: Chang Chi
poems.note: This is Bynner’s “Chang Chi (2)”, who graduated in 799.
poems.translator: trans. Witter Bynner and Kiang Kang-hu (1929)
poems.text:
Last year you went with your troops to Tibet;
And when your men had vanished beyond the city-wall,
News was cut off between the two worlds
As between the living and the dead.
No one has come upon a faithful horse guarding
A crumpled tent or torn flag, or any trace of you.
If only I knew, I might serve you in the temple,
Instead of these tears toward the far sky.

poems.title: 沒蕃故人 (Mo fan gu ren)
poems.author: Chang Chi
poems.collection: 唐詩三百首 (Three Hundred Tang Poems)
poems.text:
前年伐月支，城下沒全師。
蕃漢斷消息，死生長別離。
無人收廢帳，歸馬識殘旗。
欲祭疑君在，天涯哭此時。
